Is Mount Everest really the tallest
mountain on Earth?
Everyone learns the answer in
school, but the real answer depends
on where you place your ruler.
Measure from sea level,
and Everest wins.
Measure from the true base of the
mountain, where its rock begins,
and another giant steps forward.
Measure from the center of the
planet, and it is a different mountain again.
Three rulers, three winners.
So which one is the real champion,
and are there mountains on other
worlds that make all of them look small?
Imagine for a moment that the ocean
waters were completely drained away.
What if we measured a mountain
not from the surface of the sea,
but from the true physical base
where it rises from the crust?
Or what if we measured height from
the center of our planet toward
the open cosmos?
Suddenly, Mount Everest is no longer
alone at the top.
Other silent giants step forward
from the deep ocean floor and the
equatorial bulge of our spinning globe.
When you change the reference point,
the geography of our planet
transforms completely.
Welcome to Miya's Note,
where today we explore what truly
makes a mountain the tallest in the world.
Let us begin in the frozen realm
of the Himalayas.
Mount Everest straddles the border
between Nepal and China,
rising to an officially recognized
8,848 meters above sea level.
Near its summit, a band of limestone
holds marine fossils, the remains
of sea creatures that lived in
a shallow ocean hundreds of millions
of years ago.
How did ocean floor end up on
the rooftop of the world?
Tens of millions of years ago,
the landmass of India drifted
northward and collided with Eurasia.
That immense collision is still
taking place right beneath our feet.
As the Indian plate pushes under
the Eurasian plate, the crust
crumples and folds, shoving ancient
seabeds into the sky.
Geologists estimate that the
Himalayas still rise by a few
millimeters each year, countered
only by the destructive forces
of wind, ice, and gravity.
In terms of altitude above sea
level, Everest remains the
undisputed king of dry land.
No other summit on Earth lets a
human being stand higher above
the ocean surface.
But here is the critical question:
why did we decide that sea level
should be the ultimate judge of height?
Sea level feels natural because
human civilization grew along the coasts.
We build harbors, sail across
oceans, and watch the tides come and go.
When nineteenth-century surveyors
mapped the great mountain ranges,
the ocean surface gave every country
a shared starting line,
a universal zero mark.
It was simple, intuitive,
and remarkably convenient.
Now look at a mountain the way
an engineer would look at a skyscraper.
An architect does not measure a
building from a street curb across
town; they measure from the
foundation up to the spire.
Apply that same logic to mountains,
and a different contender takes the crown.
We must leave the freezing snows
of the Himalayas and cross thousands
of kilometers of open water to
the islands of Hawaii.
Rising from the floor of the North
Pacific Ocean is the massive
volcanic giant Mauna Kea.
To a traveler on a sandy Hawaiian
beach, it looks like a gentle,
broad-shouldered mountain rising
into the tropical clouds.
Its summit reaches 4,207 meters
above sea level, impressive,
but modest next to Everest.
It even hosts astronomical
observatories near its peak,
because the air above it is
remarkably dry and clear.
But that visible summit is only
the tip of an unimaginably massive
volcanic structure.
How did such a colossal giant form
without a collision of continents?
While Everest was born from a
head-on crash between two
continents, Mauna Kea was born
from a mantle plume,
often called a volcanic hotspot.
Deep within the Earth,
a column of intense heat melts
rock and punches through the oceanic
crust like a welder's torch.
Over millions of years,
fluid basaltic lava erupted onto
the ocean floor and cooled in the
frigid water.
Layer after layer stacked up over
the millennia, slowly building
an enormous shield volcano.
Think of Mauna Kea as an iceberg of stone.
Above the waves it stands 4,207 meters.
But its base rests about six
thousand meters below the surface
of the Pacific, so measured from
the seafloor, it rises roughly
10,210 meters, well over a thousand
meters taller than Everest.
If you were a deep-sea creature
crawling along the Pacific floor
and looking up, you would be gazing
at a stone wall more than ten kilometers high.
From this perspective, Everest
is a tall spire resting on an
already elevated continental
plateau, while Mauna Kea is the
true physical titan built up from
the ocean floor.
For a third ruler,
we must travel to the volcanic
spine of Ecuador, in South America.
Here stands Mount Chimborazo,
an ancient, ice-capped stratovolcano
in the Western Cordillera of the Andes.
By its official altitude,
Chimborazo seems entirely out of the running.
Its summit rises to 6,263 meters
above the ocean, far down the list
of global summits.
It is not even the highest peak
in the Andes; that title belongs
to Aconcagua in Argentina.
Yet Chimborazo holds a unique
planetary distinction.
Its summit is the farthest point
on the Earth's surface from the
center of our planet.
How can a mountain more than two
thousand meters shorter than Everest
reach farther into space?
The secret lies in the imperfect
shape of the Earth.
In textbooks, our planet is a
smooth, perfect blue marble.
In reality, it is an oblate
spheroid, slightly flattened at
the poles and bulging at the middle.
Our planet spins around its axis
at roughly 1,670 kilometers per
hour at the equator.
That rotation pushes the equatorial
regions outward, so the radius
at the equator is about twenty-one
kilometers longer than the radius
at the poles.
Chimborazo sits about one and a
half degrees south of the equator,
nestled right on top of this planetary bulge.
Everest sits much farther north,
at roughly twenty-eight degrees
latitude, well away from the maximum bulge.
Measured from the center of the
Earth, the summit of Chimborazo
is approximately 6,384 kilometers away.
Everest comes up short by more
than two thousand meters.
Think about that astonishing reality.
On the icy, wind-whipped peak of
Chimborazo, you would be farther
from the center of our planet than
anyone standing anywhere else on
Earth's surface.
Looking up into the clear equatorial
night sky, you would stand on the
true rooftop of Earth's geometry.
In this race outward,
a quiet South American volcano
beats Mount Everest by about two kilometers.
Isn't it remarkable how a single
question changes with your frame of reference?
Define height by sea level,
and Everest is the champion.
Measure the rise from base to peak,
and Mauna Kea stands supreme.
Measure the distance from the center
of the Earth, and Chimborazo reigns.
Nature provides no single universal
scoreboard; human beings design
it, and the results depend on the
rules we choose.
This realization forces us to look
at the opposite end of the scale.
What about the world hidden beneath
the waves, where the planet drops
into darkness?
In the western Pacific,
near the Mariana Islands,
the seabed plunges into the Mariana Trench.
At its lowest known point,
the Challenger Deep, the ocean
floor lies nearly eleven thousand
meters below the surface.
To grasp that depth,
imagine carving Mount Everest from
its roots and dropping it into
the Challenger Deep.
The entire mountain would slip
beneath the dark water,
with its summit still more than
two kilometers under the surface.
Why can ocean trenches plunge eleven
kilometers down, while our tallest
mountains rise less than nine?
Part of the answer is the strength
of rock and the pull of gravity.
A mountain is an immense load
pressing down on the Earth's crust
and the slowly flowing mantle beneath it.
Geologists suspect that a mountain
much taller than ten kilometers
would crush the rock beneath it,
forcing that rock to deform and
flow like soft plastic.
Trenches are different.
They form where one tectonic plate
dives beneath another, so they
are not piled up against gravity at all.
This raises a thrilling question:
what happens when we leave Earth entirely?
To witness the ultimate mountains
of the Solar System,
we must turn our telescopes toward
the red deserts of Mars.
Mars is a smaller world,
with only about thirty-eight percent
of our planet's surface gravity,
and it has no active plate tectonics.
Scientists think that without moving
plates, the crust stays fixed over
volcanic hotspots, letting a volcano
keep growing in one place for an
extraordinarily long time.
Olympus Mons is a planetary wonder
that defies easy comprehension.
It towers approximately twenty-one
to twenty-two kilometers above
the surrounding Martian plains.
That is about two and a half
times the height of Everest above
sea level, and more than twice
the base-to-peak height of Mauna Kea.
If you placed Olympus Mons on North
America, its circular base,
roughly six hundred kilometers
wide, would cover a region about
the size of Arizona.
Its summit caldera alone spans
dozens of kilometers across.
What would it feel like to stand
on Olympus Mons?
You might expect a jagged cliff,
but because it is a shield volcano,
its average slope is only a few degrees.
The mountain is so broad that you
would hardly realize you were
climbing; the ground would simply
tilt gently upward into a dusty sky.
Mars is not the only world with
towering stone.
On the asteroid Vesta,
a giant impact carved a crater
called Rheasilvia.
NASA's Dawn spacecraft found its
central peak rising roughly twenty
to twenty-five kilometers above
the crater floor.
On a small body with a tiny
fraction of Earth's gravity,
rock can stand far taller than
on our dense, heavy planet.
Now let us return from the cold
deserts of Mars and the quiet rocks
of the asteroid belt to our home world.
Seen from an orbit hundreds of
kilometers above the atmosphere,
Everest, Mauna Kea, and Chimborazo
all seem to disappear.
Our planet looks like a smooth,
glistening blue jewel suspended
in an ocean of darkness.
In fact, if you shrank the Earth
to the size of a billiard ball,
it would feel remarkably smooth.
The difference between the highest
peak on land and the deepest trench
in the ocean is less than twenty kilometers.
On a planet more than twelve
thousand seven hundred kilometers
across, that is a fraction of a
single percent.
The jagged peaks that have tested
human courage and claimed hundreds
of lives are microscopic textures
on the skin of our world.
So which mountain is truly the highest?
If your definition honors the human
struggle against thin air and bitter
cold, the answer is Mount Everest,
the ultimate benchmark of endurance
on dry land.
If it respects the pure scale of
geology, rising from the ocean
floor, then Mauna Kea is the monarch
of our planet.
And if it celebrates our place
in the wider universe,
looking outward, Chimborazo is
the summit that reaches farthest into space.
None of these answers is wrong.
Each represents a different ruler
and a different way of looking
at our home.
The world does not come in rigid,
pre-labeled categories, and the
questions we ask determine the
answers we receive.
When we change the baseline,
we do not change the mountain;
we change our understanding of
our place within the landscape.
The next time you sip your morning
tea or gaze out a train window
at the distant horizon,
remember that the ground beneath
you is part of a grand, spinning sphere.
Beneath the streets, tectonic plates
drift slowly over flowing rock.
Far across the blue horizons,
ancient volcanoes anchor themselves
in the deep sea,
and equatorial summits reach toward
the quiet stars.
The world is larger,
stranger, and more wondrous than
our school textbooks ever led us to believe.
